draft.title: The Australian Constitution
card: The Constitution is the set of rules that creates Australia's system of government. It came into effect on 1 January 1901, when the colonies joined to form the Commonwealth of Australia.
It sets up three institutions at the federal level: the federal parliament, the federal government and the High Court.
It also divides power between the Commonwealth (the federal level) and the states. Some powers are given to the Commonwealth, such as defence. Other matters are left mainly to the states.
The Constitution can only be changed by a referendum. A referendum is a vote in which Australian voters decide whether to accept the change.
draft.remember: The Constitution sets up the federal institutions and shares power between the Commonwealth and the states.

a.q: What is the main job of the Australian Constitution?
opts: It sets up the federal institutions and divides power
It lists the laws that each citizen must obey each day
It sets the prices of goods sold by Australian firms
It names the people who must lead each federal party
a.why: The Constitution creates the federal parliament, government and High Court, and shares power between the Commonwealth and the states. It does not list everyday laws, because ordinary laws are made later by parliaments.
a.clue: Think about what it creates and how it shares power.

b.q: A group of voters wants to change a rule in the Constitution. How can the change be made?
opts: By a referendum in which voters decide
By a vote of the federal parliament alone
By a decision of the High Court judges
By an order from the state governments
b.why: The Constitution can only be changed by a referendum, where Australian voters decide whether to accept the change. Parliament alone cannot change it, which is why it differs from an ordinary law that parliament can pass or amend.
b.clue: Who gets to vote on a change to the Constitution?

a.best: It sets up the federal institutions and divides power

b.best: By a referendum in which voters decide

problems.detail: The question says a group of voters wants to change a rule, which suggests voters can start a constitutional change themselves. In fact the federal parliament must first pass the proposed change before it goes to a referendum. Reframing it as 'How can a rule in the Constitution be changed?' would avoid this.
